prompt: The partner's API key reads the books, then asks for the list of keys and is refused. Which question did the server answer with no?
hint: It had already worked out who was asking.

choices.text: Who is this caller?
choices.why: The server knew: the key matched its row, and `/v1/whoami` names the partner. That question was answered yes.

choices.text: Has the key expired yet?
choices.why: keys.py's keys have no expiry; they last until revoked. And an expired credential is a 401, not a refusal of one action.

choices.text: Is this caller allowed to do this?
choices.why: Right. That is authorisation: a known caller, an action it may not take, and a 403.

choices.text: Was the request sent over HTTPS?
choices.why: The lab is plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1 throughout, and the same key read the books a moment before.

prompt: Match each term to what it is.
hint: One of them is a name, and a name proves nothing.

pairs.left: ana's password, or a token issued to her
pairs.right: a credential: proof of the name
deciding what that caller may do

right_distractors: a scheme the server would accept

prompt: An employee who changes prices and a partner program that reads the catalogue have both authenticated to a shop's API. What does that settle?
hint: Two questions, asked in order.

choices.text: That both may change prices, since both proved who they are
choices.why: This is the single-gate picture. Proving a name opens nothing by itself; a rule about the name and the action decides.

choices.text: Who each one is, and nothing yet about what each may do
choices.why: Right. Authentication hands the server a name; authorisation, lesson 11, decides what that name may do.

choices.text: That their requests are encrypted on the way
choices.why: Authentication says nothing about the wire. Encryption is HTTPS, lesson 13, and Basic over plain HTTP shows the two are separate.

choices.text: Which of the two the shop trusts more
choices.why: Trust is a rule somebody writes about each name, which is authorisation. Authenticating both equally says nothing about it.

prompt: After `adduser ana`, what is in the `password_hash` column of her row?
hint: Three fields joined by `$`.

choices.text: The password, encrypted with a key that keys.py keeps
choices.why: Nothing in keys.py can decrypt it, because nothing was encrypted. A hash is one-way: the server can check a password against it and never get the password back.

choices.text: The password in base64
choices.why: That is what travels in a Basic header, and anybody can decode it. Storing it would put every password one `base64 -d` away.

choices.text: A token that stands in for the password
choices.why: Tokens live in their own table, are issued at login and expire. The users table holds what checks the password itself.

choices.text: The function's name, a random salt, and the scrypt result
choices.why: Right. To check a password the server runs scrypt again with that salt and compares the results; lesson 10 is about choosing all three.

prompt: Why does `rest.py` have to be stopped before `python3 keys.py` starts?
hint: Look at the address each one listens on.

choices.text: Both listen on 127.0.0.1:8000
choices.why: Right. Only one program can hold a port; the second would fail to start. The data in shelf.db is shared without trouble.

choices.text: keys.py replaces the tables that rest.py reads
choices.why: keys.py only adds three tables with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`; the books are untouched, and rest.py reads them later as before.

choices.text: rest.py would hand out the books without any credential and so make keys.py pointless
choices.why: True of a real deployment, where the open API would be a back door, but not why it must stop here: the clash is the port.

choices.text: SQLite lets one program open shelf.db at a time
choices.why: SQLite allows many readers at once; `sqlite3 shelf.db` ran beside the server all through the lesson.

prompt: A 401 carries `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="shelf"`. What is it telling the client?
hint: It is a challenge, not an error message.

choices.text: Bearer tokens are accepted for shelf
choices.why: Right. Each `WWW-Authenticate` names a scheme the server takes, and `realm` names what it protects.

choices.text: The token it sent has expired and must be renewed
choices.why: That one came with no credential at all. A refused token adds `error="invalid_token"`, and even then does not say why.

choices.text: It has to create an account before it asks again
choices.why: A challenge says how to prove a name, not how to get one. keys.py has no sign-up at all; users are added from the command line.

choices.text: The realm called shelf is down for maintenance
choices.why: A server that is down answers 5xx or nothing. A 401 is a working server asking who you are.

prompt: A client with a valid token asks to delete another user's account, which its user may not do. Which status fits?
hint: Would sending the same credential again change anything?

choices.text: 401, so the client signs in again with more rights
choices.why: A 401 here sends the client round a login loop: it signs in, gets the same token's rights, asks, and gets a 401 again.

choices.text: 400, because the request should not have been sent
choices.why: 400 says the request is malformed. This one is well formed; what is wrong is who is making it.
Right. The server knows who is asking and refuses the action, and repeating the credential will not change it.

choices.text: 401 without `WWW-Authenticate`, since no other scheme would help
choices.why: A 401 without a challenge breaks the contract twice: wrong status, and nothing saying how to authenticate.

prompt: A client answers a challenge with the `___` header: a scheme, a space, then the credentials.
hint: Its name is a misnomer too, like 401's.

prompt: keys.py answers a request with no credential with a 401. How many `WWW-Authenticate` headers does that 401 carry?
hint: One per scheme that has a standard challenge.

prompt: curl sent `Authorization: Basic YW5hOnJpdmVyLWxhbXAtNDI=`. What does somebody who copies that header have?
hint: Try `base64 -d`.

choices.text: Only the name; the password part is encrypted
choices.why: Nothing in Basic is encrypted. The whole `name:password` is base64, and it decodes in one command.

choices.text: A hash of the password that would still have to be cracked
choices.why: The hash lives in the server's table. What travels is the password itself, encoded.

choices.text: The name and the password
choices.why: Right. base64 is an encoding, and `base64 -d` printed `ana:river-lamp-42`. That is why Basic needs HTTPS.

choices.text: Nothing they can use without the server's key
choices.why: base64 has no key. Anybody with the header has everything needed to be ana.

prompt: Which of these follow from Basic sending the password with every request? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about the server, the client and taking access away.

choices.text: The server runs its slow password check on every request
choices.why: Right. A hundred requests are a hundred scrypt runs, on both sides of the wait.

choices.text: The client must keep the password for as long as it makes requests
choices.why: Right. Whatever can read where it is kept can be ana.

choices.text: The base64 keeps the password safe on plain HTTP
choices.why: base64 decodes in one command. Only HTTPS hides the header on the way.

choices.text: Access ends only when the password changes
choices.why: Right. The server keeps nothing per client that it could delete, so there is no logout.

choices.text: The server keeps a session row that logout can delete
choices.why: That is the bearer token's table. Basic leaves nothing on the server between requests.

prompt: base64 is an ___, not encryption: it has no key, and `base64 -d` turns it back.
hint: A way of writing bytes with printable characters.

prompt: A copy of `shelf.db` leaks, `tokens` table included. Why can the rows in it not be sent as tokens?
hint: What does keys.py do with whatever arrives after `Bearer`?

choices.text: The rows are encrypted with a key only the server has
choices.why: Nothing is encrypted; the rows are hashes. Their safety comes from what the server does with what it is sent.

choices.text: A sent hash is hashed again, and that is in no row
choices.why: Right. The hash of the hash is in no row. That is the point of storing only the SHA-256.

choices.text: Tokens expire the moment the file is copied
choices.why: Copying a file changes nothing on the server. The tokens keep their expiry, up to an hour away.

choices.text: SQLite files are unreadable outside the program that made them
choices.why: `sqlite3 shelf.db` read the table in the lesson. The file is readable by anyone who has it.

prompt: keys.py stores passwords with scrypt and tokens with plain SHA-256. What makes the fast hash enough for a token?
hint: What makes a slow hash worth its cost for a password?

choices.text: Tokens expire within the hour, so a leaked hash is useless after that
choices.why: The expiry limits the token, not the work of guessing it. Even a token that lived a year would be safe behind SHA-256.

choices.text: SHA-256 is slower than scrypt
choices.why: The other way round, and by design: scrypt is slow on purpose, and that is why passwords get it.

choices.text: Nobody chose it, so there is no list of likely values to try
choices.why: Right. A slow hash makes guessing likely passwords expensive; 256 random bits leave nothing likely to guess.

choices.text: Tokens never leave the server
choices.why: They leave it on every login: the client holds the token and sends it with each request.

prompt: `TOKEN_SECONDS` in keys.py is 3600. For how many minutes after a login does the token work, if nobody logs out?
hint: Seconds to minutes.

prompt: Put the life of one keys.py token in order.
hint: The password is sent once, at the start.
items: POST `/v1/login` with the name and the password
keys.py stores the SHA-256 of a new random token
The client sends `Authorization: Bearer` with each request
The same token gets a 401 with `error="invalid_token"`
trap: The row is written before the client sees the token, and deleting it is the whole of revocation.

prompt: Why does the partner bookshop get its own API key rather than ana's name and password?
hint: Think about the day somebody leaves, and about what the log says.

choices.text: A password cannot travel in a header
choices.why: Basic puts one in `Authorization` on every request. The reason is who the credential names.

choices.text: So the requests name its program, and revoking that access touches no password
choices.why: Right. `/v1/whoami` says `application`, and revoking the key leaves ana's password alone.

choices.text: Keys never expire, so the partner never has to change anything
choices.why: Lasting until revoked is the key's weakness, not its selling point, and rotation means the partner does change it.

choices.text: ana's password would be shown by `/v1/whoami`
choices.why: `/v1/whoami` shows a kind and a name, never a credential.

prompt: `shelf_2ff69109` is stored as it is, unhashed. What is it for?
hint: It is the part of the key that is safe to show.

choices.text: Proving the key valid without needing the secret part
choices.why: Anybody can read a prefix in a log. The proof is the secret part, checked by its hash.

choices.text: Encrypting the secret part before it is stored
choices.why: Nothing is encrypted. The secret part is hashed, and the prefix is not involved in that.

choices.text: Saying how long the key lives before it expires
choices.why: keys.py's keys have no expiry; they last until somebody deletes the row.

choices.text: Finding the row, and spotting the key in logs
choices.why: Right. It is the primary key keys.py looks up, and a pattern a secret scanner can spot in a public repository.

prompt: Put the rotation of a partner's key in order, so the partner never has a moment without a working key.
hint: The old key is the last thing to go.
items: Create a second key for the partner
Pass the new key to the partner
The partner switches its configuration to the new key
Watch the old key's `last_used` stop moving
Revoke the old key by its prefix
trap: Revoking first leaves the partner refused until the new key reaches its configuration.

prompt: A partner lost the key ana made for them last month and asks for it to be sent again. What can she do with keys.py?
hint: What did the server keep of the key?

choices.text: Make a new key, pass it on, revoke the lost one
choices.why: Right. Nothing can show the old key again, and a key nobody can account for is better revoked.

choices.text: Read it from the `api_keys` table
choices.why: The table holds the prefix and a SHA-256 of the key. The key itself is in no row.

choices.text: Ask `GET /v1/keys`, which lists every key
choices.why: It lists prefixes, names and dates. The note on creation said it: shown once.

choices.text: Decode it from the stored hash with `base64 -d`
choices.why: A hash is not an encoding. base64 turns back; SHA-256 does not.

prompt: keys.py refused `?access_token=…` with a 401. Why is that token still compromised?
hint: Look at the second terminal.

choices.text: Its request line went into the server's log
choices.why: Right. Every request is logged, refused ones included, query string and all, and the token sat in the log while it was still valid.

choices.text: A 401 confirms to the caller that the token is valid
choices.why: The 401 said `authentication required`, the same as for no token. It confirmed nothing.

choices.text: keys.py copied it into the `tokens` table
choices.why: Only `/v1/login` writes that table, and it writes hashes.

choices.text: curl keeps every URL it fetches in a history file
choices.why: curl keeps no history. The leak in the capture is on the server's side.

prompt: A token was put in a URL. Where can it end up? Choose all that apply.
hint: Anywhere an address is written down.

choices.text: The access log of a proxy in front of the server
choices.why: Right. Every proxy logs the request line, and the server cannot scrub somebody else's log.

choices.text: The browser's history
choices.why: Right. An address opened in a browser is kept there, token and all.

choices.text: The `Authorization` header of the next request
choices.why: Nothing moves a query parameter into a header on its own; the header is what the client chose not to use.

choices.text: The `Referer` header sent to the next site the page links to
choices.why: Right. The browser tells the next site where the visitor came from, and that address carried the token.

choices.text: The `tokens` table, unhashed
choices.why: The table holds hashes, written at login, whatever the URL said.

prompt: A support ticket shows a URL with a live keys.py token in it. What fixes the leak?
hint: The ticket is not the only copy.

choices.text: Deleting the ticket
choices.why: The same URL is in logs and histories nobody will find. Only the server can make the token worthless.

choices.text: Waiting: it may stop working within the hour
choices.why: It will, and until then it works for whoever has the URL. An expiry bounds a leak nobody knows about; this one is known.

choices.text: Scrubbing the token out of keys.py's log
choices.why: That removes one copy of several, and the token still works.

choices.text: Revoking it with `/v1/logout`, then logging in again
choices.why: Right. Deleting the row makes every copy, wherever it is, worthless at once.

prompt: Why is `==` the wrong way to compare a key with the stored one?
hint: Compare the first two timings in the capture.

choices.text: Its time depends on where the strings differ
choices.why: Right. 19.8 nsec when the first character differed, 3.25 usec when the last did: the time depends on the answer.

choices.text: It is slower than `compare_digest` on long strings
choices.why: It is faster, in the capture by a long way. Speed is not the problem; varying speed is.

choices.text: It can say two different strings are equal
choices.why: Its answer is always right. What leaks is how long it took to give it.

choices.text: It compares only the first 43 characters of each string
choices.why: It compared all hundred thousand when they were equal up to the last one.

prompt: In the capture, `==` took 19.8 nsec when the strings differed in the first character and 3.25 usec when they differed in the last. About how many times longer was the second?
hint: One usec is a thousand nsec.

prompt: Match each language to its constant-time comparison.
hint: One of the right-hand names is an ordinary equality, and it is the trap.

prompt: Suppose `check_password` returned at once for an unknown user and skipped `DECOY`. What would the capture's timings show?
hint: Which part of the check is slow?

choices.text: Nothing new; the message would still be the same
choices.why: The words would match and the clock would not. A stopwatch reads a difference as well as a message does.

choices.text: Both refusals would get quicker
choices.why: A known user with a wrong password still runs scrypt; only the unknown one skips it.

choices.text: The unknown user's refusal would be far quicker, so the time would say the name has no account
choices.why: Right. scrypt is the slow part; skipping it for unknown names answers the forbidden question by the clock.

choices.text: The right password would take longer than before
choices.why: The right password's path never touches the decoy, so nothing changes for it.

prompt: How does keys.py's log name a refused bearer token?
hint: `ce6f21ae` was one.

choices.text: In full, so that the token can be found and revoked later
choices.why: A full token in a log is a credential in a log, readable by whoever reads logs.

choices.text: By its base64 decoding, which hides the secret part
choices.why: A token is not base64 of anything meaningful, and decoding it would hide nothing anyway.

choices.text: By the name of the user the token was issued to
choices.why: A refused token belongs to nobody the server knows; that is why it was refused.

choices.text: By a fingerprint: the start of its SHA-256
choices.why: Right. Eight characters of the hash are enough to match a row or a ticket, and useless as a credential.

prompt: The rule for every log line about a credential: it names the credential and never ___ it.
hint: A user name, a fingerprint and a prefix name one; a password, a token and a key would be in it.

prompt: Match each caller to the credential that fits it.
hint: Is somebody there, and who should the log name?

pairs.left: a partner's program syncing stock every night
a person who signs in to an app and works for an hour
a script on an internal server, over HTTPS

right_distractors: a password in the query string

prompt: A partner's integration logs in with an employee's name and password over Basic. The employee leaves. What goes wrong?
hint: Two of the three questions in the section have a bad answer here.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the partner uses HTTPS
choices.why: HTTPS protects the password on the way. It does not change whose password it is.

choices.text: Ending the leaver's access breaks the partner
choices.why: Right. Basic ends when the password changes, everywhere at once. And every request the partner made was logged as the employee, so the log never named the partner either.

choices.text: The partner gets 403 on every request from then on
choices.why: After the password changes the credential proves nothing, which is a 401, not a 403.

choices.text: The password's scrypt hash expires with the account
choices.why: Hashes have no expiry; the row stays until somebody changes or deletes it.

prompt: A keys.py token leaks in a crash report that a dozen people can read. What limits the damage?
hint: The leaked string is the token itself, not its hash.

choices.text: It is stored hashed, so the copy in the report is useless
choices.why: The hash protects against a leaked database. The report holds the token the client sends, and it works.

choices.text: Its expiry within the hour, and a logout that deletes its row now
choices.why: Right. Expiry bounds the leak nobody noticed; revocation ends the one somebody did.

choices.text: It is compared with `compare_digest`, so it cannot be replayed
choices.why: `compare_digest` hides timing. A token sent again is the same token, and it is accepted.

choices.text: It is base64, so the report shows only an encoding
choices.why: An encoding hides nothing, and a bearer token is used exactly as written.

prompt: A request arrives with an `X-API-Key` header and asks for `GET /v1/keys`. Put what keys.py does in order.
hint: Authentication finishes before authorisation starts.
items: Find the row by the key's prefix
Compare the SHA-256 of the key with `compare_digest`
Conclude the caller is an application
trap: The 403 comes last: the server has to know who is asking before it can refuse what they ask.

prompt: An API answers a failed login with 401, no `WWW-Authenticate`, and the body `no user called bob`; for debugging it logs every request header. What should change? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three sections of this lesson each find one problem.

choices.text: Answer 403 instead of 401
choices.why: No name was proved, so 401 is right; 403 is for a caller the server knows.

choices.text: Give the same message for an unknown user and a wrong password
choices.why: Right. `no user called bob` tells a stranger who has an account.

choices.text: Stop logging the `Authorization` header
choices.why: Right. Logging every header puts every password and token in the log.

choices.text: Add a `WWW-Authenticate` header to the 401
choices.why: Right. A 401 without a challenge says authenticate and not how.

choices.text: Encode the log lines in base64
choices.why: Anybody reading the log can decode them; the fix is to leave the credential out.
